purpose: New Doogh evidence leads from Iranian food-composition compilation and commercial product salt studies. Not used by enrichment, publishing, aggregation or nutrition UI.

sources.title: The relationship between nutritional facts and temperament of selected Iranians’ frequent food items: a summative content analysis study (Iranian FCT edition discrepancy)
sources.underlyingTable: Iranian Food Composition Table, National Nutrition and Food Technology Research Institute, 2018; authors also cite USDA
limitations: The article does not map each nutrient value to one of the two underlying databases
Original FCT food code and exact Doogh definition not reproduced
Summary table reports only selected highest values, not a complete Doogh record
The paper describes the Iranian FCT as published in 2018, while FAO/EuroFIR catalogs the national dataset as Iranian Food Composition Table 2017; discrepancy unresolved.
FAO/EuroFIR marks the Iranian 2017 FCT as restricted access.
Doogh sodium appears in a ranked high-sodium foods table; exact source database and food code are not identified.

sources.title: Salt Contents in Fermented Dairy Products: A Strategic Blueprint for Healthier Intake
sources.sampleDescription: 79 industrial fermented dairy products sampled in five Tehran food-chain stores in 2024; Doogh n=6.
sources.methods: Potentiometric titration for NaCl after homogenization; oven drying for moisture; analysis in triplicate.
limitations: Industrial products may not represent the GrowFit source definition
Salt and moisture only, not full micronutrient panel

sources.title: Microbial and Chemical Characteristics of Doogh (Iranian Fermented Milk Drink)
sources.sampleDescription: 60 commercial Doogh samples and 88 Kefir samples purchased in multiple Iranian cities, Jan–Mar 2021.
sources.methods: Standard salt testing; reverse-phase HPLC-UV for preservatives; fungal counts.
limitations: Table 2 labels salt values mg/L while comparing with a standard in g/100mL
Numerical salt values not safely normalizable until unit discrepancy is resolved

sources.title: Evaluation and Comparison the Physicochemical Properties Pasteurized Kefir and Doogh
limitations: Calcium and phosphorus results conflict with ash and are not accepted

observations.basis: reported per 100g in secondary analysis; exact FCT record not identified
reviewNotes: The paper says it used the 2018 Iranian FCT and USDA but does not state which database supplied the Doogh values.
The reported water value is broadly compatible with GrowFit's diluted drink definition but does not prove identity.
Need original Iranian FCT food code and complete record before publication.
FAO/EuroFIR catalog the national Iranian FCT as 2017 (restricted access), while the article says 2018; exact edition discrepancy unresolved.
The 421 mg/100g sodium value is from a ranked summary, not a complete Doogh source row, and may derive from either Iranian FCT or USDA.
Do not convert salt to sodium for food-bank publication without explicit reviewed conversion.
Industrial product samples are not necessarily the GrowFit recipe.

observations.basis: table labels mg/L; compared against g/100mL standard
reviewNotes: Unit conflict makes this result non-normalizable; retain only as a bibliographic warning, not a nutrient candidate.

observations.basis: percentage in sampled product; exact as-consumed basis unclear
reviewNotes: Macros disagree substantially with GrowFit base macros.
Calcium/phosphorus rows rejected due to unit/balance concerns.
